Regarding this term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the characteristic of the name itself; it does not mean that there is a separate substantial characteristic existing apart from the name. It may also refer to the characteristic as conceptualized by [false] discrimination.
From "Second, for those who practice meditation... onwards, the conclusion exhorts one to awaken to and enter [the truth]. Thus far, [the argument] has relied upon inference (*anumāna*).
The wisdom accomplished through the power of investigation and discernment realizes the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Next, secondly, based on the power of cultivation, one realizes the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Regarding the initial [section], this refers to those who have already ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*).
This is determined by the subsequent text of this treatise, which indicates that although there is contaminated wisdom of cultivation prior to the stages, [it is distinguished] because...

The wisdoms of hearing and reflection are for the purpose of severing delusions on the stages (bhūmi); these are judged to be the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). This is explained in detail in the lower fascicle.

Regarding [the entry into reality], although one enters through the power of the wisdom of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-jñāna-bala*), it is by means of the functional application of the power of the wisdom of cultivation that—just as when a bird’s wings and feathers have first grown—one can, by inference, know how to fly in the void; yet one is not yet able to do so.

Just as the wisdom that discriminates through investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna-jñāna*), though it inferentially knows that the nature of all phenomena is empty, has not yet realized it directly—so too is this [case].

Below, in the second section, the text correctly clarifies the realization of the emptiness of the nature of phenomena by relying on the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). Within this passage, furthermore...
Two. First, it clarifies the correct realization of the emptiness of intrinsic nature by relying on the power of [the preceding].

Second, from "In this way, practicing correctly" onwards, one understands non-arising by analogy through realizing the nature of emptiness; herein there are again two parts: first, it clarifies the realization of the emptiness of intrinsic nature by relying on cultivation;

second, from "As the World-Honored One said" onwards, it cites scriptural statements to establish the proof. Regarding the former, there are four sections: first, the Dharma; second, the simile; third, the application; and fourth, the conclusion.
The four fetters. Regarding the first statement, "therefore one again applies oneself with diligence through the power of cultivation," this refers to the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi.

Although one possesses the power of wisdom from analytical reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and knows by inference that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), one has not yet relied upon the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path of the bhūmis to realize the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*). Now, within the dharmas of the worldly-first [stage], one cultivates the three...
□□ Attaining the first bhūmi, one cultivates true contemplative practice (*bhāvanā*). When it first manifests before one, one realizes the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*);

therefore, it is said that [this arises from] the power of repeated cultivation and practice. Second, the passage beginning with "like a physician suffering from ophthalmia" is a metaphorical illustration.

It refers to ordinary beings prior to the stages (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi-pūrva*), who are blinded by the distinctions of perceived characteristics (*nimitta*). This is like a person without eyes entering the darkness; they see nothing at all. Therefore...

Regarding the phrase "like an oculist": by administering medicine that can remove cataracts, the eyes become pure and clear, and one perceives objects with clarity, free from flies, mosquitoes, and the like.

This means that by applying the medicine of true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), one is able to dispel the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Thus, the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) becomes clear, and one perceives reality with clarity, free from the grasping of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The nature is empty. [The following] corresponds to the analogy. "Diligently practicing... corresponds to obtaining the remedy that can eliminate the disease of visual impairment;
it corresponds to eliminating the grasping at conditioned phenomena through the wisdom of non-arising.

This precisely corresponds to the aforementioned disease of visual impairment to be eliminated. When the true contemplative practice first manifests, one receives [realization] without depending on other conditions.
Sublime joy and bliss. This corresponds to the preceding [attainment of] purity of the eyes. It is not through other conditions that one experiences sublime joy and bliss;
rather, it is by means of the eye and its objects as conditions that one experiences joy and bliss pervading the body and mind. This is precisely the realization of the first [dhyāna].
Because one grasps all conditioned marks, this corresponds to the preceding [removal of] coarse flies and the like. Constantly...
The cultivation of the Great [Vehicle] corresponds to the previously explained "seeing the realm. Within the former, there are two parts. First, a general explanation of non-appropriation:
"All conditioned phenomena are not to be appropriated," and so forth. Second, a specific explanation of non-appropriation.

Within this section on non-appropriation, there are three parts: first, explaining non-deluded appropriation; second, [from "not deludedly seeking" onwards], explaining non-deluded seeking; third, [from "not [seeking]" downwards].
This clarifies the absence of false attachment. Within the preceding section on the absence of false grasping, the first part clarifies the non-apprehension of the three wheels;

the second, from "is able to" (*neng*) downward, clarifies the non-apprehension of the two adornments. Within the first [section] on the three wheels, there are two parts: the first explains the wheel of the giver by way of the cause of giving;
the second generally explains the three wheels by way of the fruit of giving. Regarding the initial statement that one does not grasp at the gift: this means realizing that all phenomena are empty.
Regarding the giver and the receiver, one realizes the emptiness of the *pudgala* (person); this means that at the time of giving, nothing is grasped.
Second, [the text] further clarifies the emptiness of the *sattva* (sentient being) as well as the emptiness of the dharmas regarding the karmic retribution of giving.

There are two types of retribution: first, the present retribution consisting of respect and offerings; second, the future retribution consisting of both the primary and secondary fruits (*āśraya-vipāka* and *parivāra-vipāka*).
"Not grasping at the giver" means realizing that the substance of the giver who will experience the future fruit is empty.
"The recipient" means realizing that the substance of the recipient who is able to receive the retribution is empty. "The gift" means realizing that the substance of the respectful offering is empty.
Regarding the two kinds of threefold wheels attaining purity: this refers to being free from conceptual proliferation, which is termed "purity."
Second, "is able to apply oneself with right diligence" and so forth clarifies not grasping at the two adornments.

Because one realizes that the three wheels are empty in their essence and has lost all sense of self and other, one is able to apply oneself with diligent effort. One gathers immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom, which serve as the burden to be carried.
These two [provisions] constitute the "provisions" during the causal stage; when they reach fruition, they are called "bodhi," having the three bodies as its essence. This is the primary tenet.
Respectfully bearing the burden, one will ultimately attain the fruit; therefore, it is called a "heavy burden. This is as the Sūtra says:
"This person can bear the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Second, "never lowering [the burden]" clarifies that one does not seek falsely.
Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying that one does not falsely crave or seek the present, outflowing fruits of the three realms.
Second, "nor does it descend" clarifies that there are no outflows (*āsrava*) because the fruit has not yet manifested. Third, "nor does it falsely cling to descending" clarifies non-attachment.
Regarding the statement, "The one who creates the qualities is the agent;

the self is the experiencer," this refers to the Sāṃkhya school, which calculates that the three qualities (*guṇa*)—suffering, pleasure, and delusion—are the creators, while the self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer who experiences them.
This is what is offered to virtue. As for the statement "I am the agent," this refers to the Vaiśeṣikas, who reckon that the self (ātman) is both the agent and the experiencer;

therefore, they say "I am the agent. Alternatively, there are non-Buddhists who reckon that the Great Self (Mahātmā) or the Lord (Īśvara) can create all things, and who reckon that the atoms (paramāṇu) are eternal, remaining scattered in empty space when the kalpa is destroyed.
At that time, through harmony, one is able to accomplish all things. "Nature" refers to the nature of the world;

it means that all phenomena each possess their own essence, which arises from the future and enters the present, and further flows from the present into the past. Second, regarding the constant cultivation of great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*):
[this concerns] the fruit of the objective realm, namely, realizing the non-duality of phenomena and attesting to the equality of emptiness, such that no phenomenon can be grasped.
[He] takes [them]. Therefore, it is said: "Constantly cultivating... and so forth. Below this, the conclusion establishes the basis for the proof.
This means that by means of the correct principles taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one either realizes awakening through gradual cultivation or attains it directly;

all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as well as the object of negation and the negating agent, are empty of intrinsic nature. This refers to the Buddhas of the past and present, and those yet to come.
This refers to the future Buddha. As stated below in the second citation from the *Sūtra on Proving the Accomplishment*, three sūtras and a single word state:
"A bodhisattva should not abide in any phenomena while practicing generosity.

This means that because one practices generosity by penetrating the emptiness of all things, one does not abide in one's own self while practicing generosity; one practices generosity without abiding in anything at all.
Because one realizes that all things are empty, one practices giving without dwelling upon the retribution of its fruits. This sutra clearly elucidates the emptiness of both persons and phenomena.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said: "If a bodhisattva still conceives the notion of a 'sentient being,' they should not be called a true bodhisattva.
Here, "sentient being" (*sattva*) was formerly translated as "living beings" (*zhòngshēng*). "Conceives" (*zhuǎn*) means to arise.

That is to say, if there is a bodhisattva who, toward all sentient beings, gives rise to a [conceptualizing] mind and reckons that there are "sentient beings," one should not say that this bodhisattva is called one who possesses non-erroneous, true wisdom.
This sutra merely clarifies the emptiness of the *pudgala* (person).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said: "There is not even the slightest dharma that can be named as being able to [attain] the Bodhisattva Vehicle."
This means that the Bodhisattva knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are identical to the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all dharmas.

Within this emptiness and suchness, what conditioned phenomenon could there be that serves as the "vehicle" by which one proceeds, or as the "destination" to be reached? The following uses the superior to illustrate the inferior:
because emptiness, bodhi, and saṃsāra are all entirely equal, there is nothing to delight in nor anything to loathe. This...

The sutra clarifies only the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which serves as testimony for the practice of wisdom through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) from the first bhūmi upward. Thus, one should know that the wisdom of cultivation exists only on the [bodhisattva] stages.
The preceding section has clarified how, by relying on the power of [the two accumulations], one correctly realizes the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
From here below begins the second category: the realization that all phenomena are unarisen, up to their equality.

The text [explains] how one realizes the non-arising of phenomena by relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*). Second, as in the passage beginning "If someone asks," it cites scriptural teachings to establish this proof.

Within the first section, since the two types of non-arising are absent, the three times are also absent. Because the three times are absent, the previous three [perfections], such as giving (*dāna*), are likewise absent.

"Having purified the wheel and entered the path toward great bodhi, one has correctly cultivated the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). This concludes the preceding section.
Furthermore, one should correctly contemplate that if things are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), they have no arising. This introduces what follows.
If all phenomena have been empty of their own essence from the very beginning, then within emptiness, what phenomenon could possibly arise? Therefore, it is said that there is "no arising."
Furthermore, secondly, because there is no arising, there are no three periods of time. Now, all phenomena of the three periods of time must necessarily have an initial arising and a final cessation.

Since they are now equal and entirely empty, and emptiness has no arising, and since the phenomena of arising do not exist, how can the three periods of time be established? How could they possibly be obtained?
Therefore, it is said that there is no past, future, or present. Since they are all equally empty, there is no differentiation between the three periods of time.

Thus, it is said that there is no obstruction regarding the three periods of time. By correctly contemplating the three periods of time as being free from the defilement of grasping at existence, non-existence, and other such conceptual attachments, it is said that they are all of a pure nature. Third, based on what was previously explained, there is no inversion.
Through the principle of the two-fold emptiness and the practice of the three wheels of purity—such as giving—one proceeds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This proceeding is proceeding by way of non-proceeding; it is also designated by the provisional name "enlightenment" through the absence of [intrinsic] attainment.

From here below is the second section: citing scriptural authority to establish the proof. For example, there is a question regarding Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s progression toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

This question concerns the characteristics of the causal practices that enable one to progress toward enlightenment. The answer states: “Brahmā... [progresses] toward enlightenment. This is Mañjuśrī’s response;
it refers to the essential nature of the practice that enables one to reach and progress toward [enlightenment], as follows: [The text continues: ...as if... [the passage continues].
If the fruit is indeed equal and impartial, without any distinction, then such a bodhisattva is truly able to advance toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This "advancing" is merely a conventional designation for advancing. Again, it is asked: what is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*)?
This question concerns the characteristics of the fruit of enlightenment. The answer is: it is not past, future, or present; that is to say, because all phenomena are empty.

Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is no arising. Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, there is no arising. How could there be the three periods of time? The essence of bodhi is likewise so:
it is devoid of intrinsic nature, devoid of arising, and devoid of the three periods of time and so forth. Since these share the same dharma-nature, this is the characteristic of bodhi.
Therefore, the following concludes by exhorting one to practice and study; that is to say, the equality of cause and effect is suchness (*tathatā*), and there is no distinction between them.
When a Bodhisattva practices and advances toward Bodhi, they should contemplate that the three periods of time are entirely pure, devoid of the defiled marks of arising and ceasing.
When practicing such deeds as giving, they realize the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two kinds of emptiness and engage in the practice of the purity of the three wheels.
Because there is thus no practice, no advancement, and no Bodhi, these are merely designated by name as "practice," "advancement," and "Bodhi. This is true Bodhi.

Svāhā. Thus far, the first [section] clarifies that this brief treatise was composed based on the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), so that practitioners may, by means of the three types of wisdom—namely, that derived from hearing and so forth—realize that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is entirely empty.

From here below is the second section, which, based on the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), composes this brief treatise so that practitioners may, through the three types of wisdom—namely, that derived from hearing and so forth—realize and enter into the fact that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena is emptiness. This text consists of two parts.

The first concerns how the practitioner, by means of the power of correct inference based on the wisdom accomplished through hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī prajñā*), realizes the emptiness of the nature of the unconditioned.

Second, although one has already realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) through the power of having established the stages of wisdom, because one lacks the power of superior cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*), one is unable to permanently sever that which ought to be eliminated.

Therefore, one again applies oneself with diligence to cultivate the power of superior cultivation. Below, it is explained how, by relying on the wisdom produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), one correctly enters into the unconditioned emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Within this section, there are three parts; first, a general explanation of relying on the wisdom produced by hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī*).
1. By means of correct inference (*samyak-anumāna*), one realizes and enters into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Below this, the two masters of the *Vibhāṣā* all raise this objection.

[The following] separately clarifies how, by relying on the wisdoms produced from hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*), through correct inference, one enters into the emptiness of the nature of the unconditioned as it is grasped by oneself and others.
2. Thus, having eliminated various faults and objections, the following is a summary and exhortation. Regarding the first, the general section:

The text consists of two parts. The first states, "If one does not reveal and show [this], up until the end it shall not be accomplished," clarifying the fault of failing to reveal it.

The second part, beginning with "For the sake of revealing and showing," clarifies the opening of the school for the benefit [of others]. It says: "The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) has no reality; its non-arising is like a flower in the sky.
The unconditioned is the dharma of non-existence, and "having no reality" is the dharma of existence. Thus, the dharma and the existent dharma are not separate from one another.
The title is *Zhong* (The Establishment). "Not arising" is the formulation of the reason (*hetu*). "Like a flower in the sky" is the example based on commonality (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Third, within this section, the verse is explained by relying upon the thesis (*pakṣa*). This passage consists of five parts: first, explaining the necessity of relying on the meaning of the thesis; second, from "Because it is in terms of true nature" onwards, the actual explanation of the verse by relying on the thesis;
third, from "It does not state a negation" onwards, the explanation of the purpose of the example of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); fourth... [text continues].
How is the inference (*anumāna*) established herein? Fifth, regarding "the establishment [of the thesis] set forth here," this clarifies that the inclusion of the reasons (*hetu*) is exhaustive.
This consists of two parts: first, the actual presentation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) upon which it relies, namely, "because it is the true nature" (*tattva*);

thus, the words of the thesis-formulation used for differentiation herein refer to the aforementioned "true nature. Second, the clarification of the necessity for such differentiation; therefore, it says "must."

To briefly clarify the meaning: it should be understood as previously stated. That is to say, according to what is commonly known through conventional study, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) exist.
If one were to assert that they are empty in relation to the conventional, it would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), worldly consensus, one’s own teachings, and other such criteria.

For this reason, when we now speak of the emptiness of the unconditioned, we are defining the unconditioned within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the principle of true nature.
It is emptiness. This should be understood as already clarified in the preceding upper fascicle.

From here below is the second section, which explains the verse according to our own school (*siddhānta*). Within this, there are two parts. First, the direct clarification that, according to the school of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established as emptiness;
it does not mean that the conventional teaching speaks of the unconditioned as empty. Second, from "Because it is not conditioned" onwards, the direct...

Commentary on the Verses. This section consists of three parts: first, the commentary on the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, from "In this very [context]" onwards, the commentary on the establishment of the reason (*hetu*);

and third, from "A flower in the sky has no reality" onwards, the commentary on the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Within the commentary on the establishment of the thesis, there is first the commentary on the subject (*dharmin*), followed by [the commentary on the predicate] from "In this very [context]" onwards.

Next, the exposition of that dharma. Within the exposition of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, there are three parts. First is the explanation of the name: because they are not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are called "unconditioned.
This is the meaning of "unconditioned" as the opposite of "conditioned," meaning they are not acted upon by the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth;
thus they are named unconditioned. Furthermore, they are not acted upon by the four conditions (*pratyaya*); thus they are named unconditioned. Second...

Discriminating the essence: this refers to space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the nature of suchness (*tathatā*).

That is to say, it is the portion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) that was excluded from the twelve spheres previously analyzed; the detailed analysis is as before.
Third, regarding the four unconditioned [phenomena], one must first realize that the nature of space is empty. There are two reasons for this: first, because it is easy to open [to understanding].

Furthermore, there are other reasons: namely, because it is that which is produced (*kṛtaka*), because it is not that which produces (*akāraka*), and because it is subject to destruction (*vināśa*).

By citing these four in mutual relation, the intrinsic natures of the objects to be negated are manifold, and the causes that negate them are likewise manifold. Up to this point, the general explanation has been provided.
Based on the power of correct inference derived from the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection, one realizes the emptiness of the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

This would result in establishing a meaningless position; therefore, it is said that if the thesis being established were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and lacked substantial reality, it would be non-existent.

Second, by citing the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*), existence is proven and non-existence is refuted. Thus it is said: "How can the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space exist if it has no object of perception (*ālambana*)?

What is called the 'sphere of infinite space' is the stage of the sphere of infinite space within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). 'Meditative attainment' refers to the attainment of the sphere of infinite space."

Regarding the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*): when about to enter this absorption, one first gives rise to a mind directed toward the stage of the sphere of infinite space prior to the actual concentration.

During the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realm of space as the object. If this unconditioned realm of space were not real, it would constitute a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) without a dharma, and thus there would be no objective support (*ālambana*).
Since the object of the concentration would then be non-existent, how could there be such a meditative attainment? The second objection states: "However..."
Regarding the statement "non-obstruction is the characteristic of space," this is the author's own exposition of his understanding.

Since non-obstruction actually exists as the characteristic of space, how can one say it does not exist? Within this [section], one should establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to prove that space exists.
According to the text cited by the Master of the Treatise below, there must certainly be an inference (*anumāna*).
Second, "If this [space] were a conditioned phenomenon," and so forth, the Master of the Treatise refutes [the opponent]. Within this refutation, there are four parts:

first, the refutation of the objection regarding the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite space; second, "This, with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),... and so forth, the refutation of the second objection that non-obstruction is the characteristic of space;

third, "Furthermore, precisely by means of... and so forth, the repeated refutation of the initial objection; fourth, "Therefore, my previous... and so forth, the establishment of one's own position. Within the first part, there is...

2. First, he restates the two types of inference established by the opponent, namely, the dual presentation of two propositions (*pakṣa*), two reasons (*hetu*), and two similar examples (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding the statement, "The meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*) truly possesses an object of cognition": the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space is the *dharmin* (the subject);

"it is a meditative concentration that possesses an object of cognition" is the *dharma* (the predicate). That is to say, the object of cognition of this concentration is precisely empty space (*ākāśa*). There is no [other]...

Regarding "dharma" (attribute): the non-separation of a dharma and a *dharmī* (substratum) is called a thesis (*pakṣa*). This is one type of thesis. Alternatively, [the thesis is] that the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Here, the object of cognition is the *dharmī*, and substantial existence is the dharma; the non-separation of the dharma and the *dharmī* is called the thesis.
This constitutes a formal thesis (*pakṣa*). In the first case, meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is the subject (*dharmin*); in the latter, the object of space (*ākāśa*) is the subject.
In the first case, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the property (*dharma*); in the latter, the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) is the property.

"Because it is such an attainment" is the logical reason (*hetu*) established below; this is the reason for the initial thesis. That is to say, it establishes the property of the preceding thesis through the proof of the meaning of the phenomenon.
The thesis that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*) is established by means of the reason [that they are states of meditative attainment].

Taking "being a state of meditative attainment" (*samāpatti*) as the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), since there exists a cause consisting of a state of meditative attainment that possesses an object of cognition, and since such a state of meditative attainment necessarily has an object of cognition—which may be the very object of that attainment—this constitutes the second thesis and its reason.

Previously, that which is non-existent was established as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). Now, that which is the object of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is taken as the reason (*hetu*).
To clarify the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it says "as in other meditative attainments. This refers to the first similar instance:

namely, just as in the case of the four dhyānas and the three higher formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the objects of those other meditative attainments are all existent. [The term] "empty" [is used here to indicate the absence of a counter-example].

Why is it that only the object of focus for the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*) is non-existent? Or, as for those who take it as their object—this is the same logical argument and analogy below:
namely, just as those seven [attainments] already exist, why would one clarify that the objects of focus for the attainments of the sphere of infinite space and so forth are existent?
This is stated to clarify that all the meditative attainments and the objects of focus for those attainments are entirely existent. The sphere of infinite space...

[The section on] emptiness concludes. Thus, regarding the homologous example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) you have cited, since its nature is itself empty, there is no fault of lacking a homologous example.

This explanation of the characteristics of space from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) refutes your second [position]: that the characteristic of space is the absence of obstruction by objects.

Because it arises. Second, from the words "this statement" [onward], he levels a fault against the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrin*). There are two types of faults: [first,] he charges the Master with the fault of contradicting his own tenets (*siddhānta-virodha*). He says:
"The Master asserts that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack reality because they do not arise; thus, they are called 'unreal'."

I also infer this meaning from these words: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) must be substantially real (*dravyasat*). Furthermore, since space (*ākāśa*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), gives rise to a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), it must exist as a substantial reality.
If it were a substantial reality, the Master [Vasubandhu] would incur the fault of contradicting his own two tenets that conditioned and unconditioned phenomena have no substantial existence.
Third, regarding the phrase "if one says 'it arises,'" [the opponent] provides a reason for the Master that is not universally applicable (*avyāpaka*).

In the case of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there is the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*). If one says that "arising" is also without reality, then the reason "non-arising" commits the fallacy of not pervading the similar instance.
Regarding the non-establishment of the nature of the reason: both "arising" and "non-arising" are equally without reality.

The Master [Nāgārjuna] establishes the reason by speaking only of "non-arising," yet this commits the fallacy of not pervading "arising. Therefore, he speaks of "both. This is the definitive determination.

In response to this, [the opponent] answers separately that there is the fault of the reason not being present in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*). For this reason, the reason fails to function as a valid reason.
Second, regarding "this is an implication" (*arthāpatti*) below, the Master first provides a general clarification:

"This is an implication" constitutes a fallacy of similarity, resembling the fallacy of a non-established reason (*asiddha-hetu*), rather than being a case of the two actual fallacies of non-establishment. First, in answering the charge of contradicting one's own tenets (*siddhānta-virodha*), it says:
"You should carefully determine my statement. I am simply saying that all those things which do not arise are entirely without reality;

I am not saying that whatever is determined to be without reality must necessarily not arise. Therefore, even though one can indeed give rise to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), how does this preclude their lack of reality?
Thus, there is no fault. Second, [the phrase] 'even though one exerts effort' and so forth answers the objection that the reason is not present in all similar instances."
This is not the fault of an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*). Now, let us cite the method of the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*.

It is said that a reason is established as valid when it is "necessarily present in similar instances" (*sapakṣe sattvam*). Thus, even though the reason "produced by volitional effort without interval" does not pervade all similar instances, it is still accepted as a valid reason.
Since it does not [currently] pervade them, there is likewise no fault.
There are others who further state [the following], which refutes the third attachment. This passage contains two parts. First, it introduces the externalist attachment.
