Second, it clarifies that flowers also possess an essence; for instance, the *utpala* and other such flowers are seen by the world to have an existent essence.
Therefore: (3) "The two flowers in the sky" below provides a double conclusion. It asserts that the flowers in the sky exist;

that is to say, although the two types—emptiness and the flowers—are of different natures and do not combine or correspond, these two things—the emptiness and the flowers—do not lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because each possesses its own nature.

(4) "Therefore, the analogy of the flower" below concludes that it is not the Master of the Treatise [who holds this view]. That is to say, he asserts that both emptiness and the flower each possess their own nature, yet establishes them as non-existent.

Regarding the "real," this argument is not established. Second, from "this objection is not so" onwards, the Master of the Treatise refutes it. Within this section, there are two parts: first, the direct refutation of space;

second, from "by this," the analogical refutation of cessation and non-cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). In the former, there are two sub-sections. First, the general rejection of the opponent's position; thus he says, "it is not so.
Second, "this flower in the sky is not [the object] for which [analysis] is performed"; regarding this "analysis" (*vicaya*), the commentary states: "this flower in the sky..."

Metaphor. Regarding the sixth [case], the *ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*, according to the etymological analysis of the term "basis" (*āśraya*): among the eight case-inflections (*vibhakti*), the sixth is the genitive, the "possessive" or "belonging-to" case.
As for the "eight cases": the first is called the "substantive" (*nāman*) case, which refers to the differentiation of the essence (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.

The second is called the "object" (*karman*) case, referring to that which is acted upon; for example, "cutting a tree" is an object. The third is called the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) case, such as the hand.
The first is called the "instrumental sound," such as an axe and so forth. The fourth is called the "purposeful sound," such as breaking down a tree for the purpose of building a house.
The fifth is called the "causal sound," such as the place from which something originates. The sixth is called the "possessive sound," such as saying "sky-flower";
here, "sky" is the possessor and "flower" is the possessed, meaning it is the flower of the sky, hence it is called a "sky-flower. The seventh is called the "locative sound," namely—
Whatever is produced must necessarily have a basis. The eighth is called the "direct-address" (āmantrita) tone, which refers simply to calling out to an object situated before one.
If these three tones—masculine, feminine, and neuter—each possess these eight [variations], they combine to form twenty-four modulations.

Based on these eight case-inflections (*vibhakti*), there are further six types of etymological analysis (*nirukti*), namely the six types such as *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).

If one were to analyze this term "empty flower" (*śūnyapuṣpa*) according to the eight case-inflections, it would fall under the sixth inflection, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*), which expresses possession.

Here, "emptiness" (*śūnya*) is the possessor and "flower" (*puṣpa*) is the possessed; thus, it is "the flower of emptiness," and is therefore called an "empty flower. According to the explanation of these six types of syntactic relations, it should be...
This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. That is to say, these are flowers that are empty; therefore, they are called "empty flowers.

Both of these explanations mean that the flower is itself emptiness; it is not that there is a flower existing separately outside of emptiness. Since this [flower] does not exist, as for the statement that the metaphor is "not non-existent":
because this metaphor of the empty flower is not existent, the establishment of my metaphor of the empty flower is successful; hence, it is said to be "not non-existent. Second, by...
Below this, the same logic is applied to refute the emptiness of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and so forth.

That is to say, by means of the analogy of a flower in the sky and the principle that it lacks intrinsic substance, the practitioner of meditation, following the analogy, understands all phenomena; they should correctly awaken to and enter into the fact that the unconditioned nature of space is empty.

Once one knows that the unconditioned nature of space is empty of substance, one should likewise understand that the unconditioned natures of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*, *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*, and *tathatā* are also empty in their nature. This is the path.
One should likewise realize the principle. Above, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of space was correctly refuted.

Below this, the fourth section concerns the correct refutation of the unconditioned of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) by the Vaibhāṣika masters. This passage contains three parts; first, the presentation of the objection.
Within the presentation of the objection, there are two sections; first, the explanation of the grounds for presenting the objection, namely, the inability to endure the refutation.

[The opponent] takes *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) as an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomenon. Furthermore, he raises this objection below, which correctly clarifies the formal objection.

Within this objection, there are two ways in which the opponent charges the Master with the fault of contradicting his own tenets (*viruddhārtha-doṣa*). First, by examining his own teachings, he demonstrates the contradiction: "In your Mahāyāna..."
The Buddha taught that there is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) which acts as an antidote to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and possesses great efficacy.

To slander this by claiming it does not exist is to incur the fault of contradicting one's own teachings. Second, regarding the phrase "accompanied by joy and greed," this distinguishes the contradiction based on the teaching concerning the fruit.

That is to say, when craving in the present life ceases, through the cessation of this craving, one attains the fruit of nirvāṇa, which is peaceful and sublime bliss. If one slanders this by claiming it does not exist, it is likewise [a contradiction].

The fault of contradicting one's own teachings. Second, from "In this regard, below... the author of the treatise provides a refutation. First, he refutes the fault of contradicting his own teachings. Within this section, there are two parts:

first, explaining and reconciling the Buddha’s teachings based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); second, explaining and reconciling his own statements based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Within the former, there are again two parts: first, explaining the intended meaning of the sūtras; second, from "As the Buddha said... onwards, citing scriptural statements to establish the proof. Regarding the first...
Regarding the reason why the Buddha spoke here of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):

it is to cause sentient beings to develop weary detachment toward conditioned objects and to give rise to affection and delight toward unconditioned objects. Therefore, from the perspective of conventional truth, he spoke of analytical cessation, nirvāṇa, as being quiescent, subtle, and sublime.
As stated below, "As the Buddha said," the following citation is introduced to establish this through scriptural proof: "The Buddha spoke of spontaneously born sentient beings."

This refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) experienced between the aggregates of death and the aggregates of birth; such an intermediate being is called a "beings of miraculous birth" (*upapāduka*), because this intermediate birth occurs only through miraculous transformation.

The term "sentient being" (*sattva*) is used here according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it is a provisional designation applied to the five aggregates, for there is no substantially existent sentient being.
The same applies to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): it is merely provisionally said to exist based on worldly convention.
Now, relying on what the Buddha has taught, I also accept that this unconditioned state of analytical cessation exists conventionally; therefore, there is no fault of contradicting our own tenets.

Second, the explanation and resolution of the Master’s own words according to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). This section contains two parts: first, establishing the reasoning based on our own tenets.

Therefore, it is said that [the statement] merely negates *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) with respect to its true nature (*tattva*). Second, regarding the passage "Hence the Blessed One said," etc., this cites scriptural authority to establish the proof; the text is easy to understand.

Second, regarding the passage "Furthermore, there is no denial," etc., this refutes the fault of contradicting the teaching on the fruit (*phala*). This also has two parts: first, relying on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), explaining and reconciling the Buddha’s teachings;

second, regarding the passage "It is not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)," etc., explaining and reconciling one's own words. Within the former, first is the general clarification.
There is no fault of slandering the noble truth of cessation. First, "By resorting to the conventional" explains why there is no fault.
Second, "Not by resorting to the ultimate" relies on the ultimate truth to explain how one's own words are consistent; the textual structure is easily understood.
Third, "Therefore, based on this scriptural teaching" restates both the teaching and the reasoning to conclude that there is indeed no fault.

Below the section on "Other Unwholesome Correct Reasoning," the fifth position is refuted. This passage contains two parts: first, the presentation of the opponent's objection; second, the master’s response to it.
Within the first part, it is stated that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lacks substantial reality. Since the unconditioned does not exist, the thesis (*pakṣa*) being established cannot be proven.
This constitutes a fault in the thesis, specifically the fault of the subject (*dharmin*) not being admitted by both parties (*aprasiddha*). Since the thesis being established is thus unproven...
The reason why the basis does not arise is likewise unestablished; this is a fault of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*), specifically the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Because a sky-flower does not exist, the example of "similar property" (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished. To say that the "property-possessor" (*dharmin*) is unestablished means that the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are all unestablished.
In this context, it is because the property-possessor is non-existent that they are unestablished. Thus, I have here [stated] that the property-possessor is unestablished.

This objection is untenable; the following section refutes it. First, within the refutation of the faults in the established thesis, the author clarifies that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are existent dharmas.

Second, regarding the phrase "the power of conceptual designation" in the opponent's objection, he explains that the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena—such as discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and so forth—all exist by virtue of being conceptually designated through the power of conventional mental construction. Thus, these four [exist].
They are categories. Furthermore, they are "conceivable" names; that is to say, based on conventional designations (*saṃvṛti-prajñapti*), it is said that these four exist.

In the text, each of the names for the four unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas is explained individually. The conclusion regarding their provisional establishment (*prajñapti*) can be understood. Below, the distinctions [between them] are not explicitly revealed.

This explains away the objection. The objection states: "If the Master of the Treatise establishes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as conventional (*prajñapti*), while I establish the unconditioned as real (*dravya*), then the thesis being established suffers from the fault of not being universally accepted (*aprasiddha*).
Therefore, the present explanation says: "The distinction is not explicitly stated due to the force of common consensus."

They are collectively established as "the subject" (*dharmin*). This refers to the method of establishing the subject according to the rules of logic (*hetuvidyā*), which does not reveal the specific distinctions between the characteristics of the subject's essence;
rather, it establishes something as the subject by taking the general sense of its existence from both one's own and the opponent's perspective.

Thus, when I take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to be conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*) and you take the unconditioned to be ultimately existent (*paramārthasat*), although the conventional and ultimate levels differ, the sense of its existence is no different. Therefore...
According to the rules of Hetuvidyā (Logic), this is termed the "force of common consensus"; therefore, it is established in general as the *dharmin* (the subject).

The explanation of the *dharmin* is now complete. Below, the *dharma* (the predicate) is explained. Herein, the absence of real existence is taken as the *dharma*. Regarding the statement that "the qualification which excludes what is not commonly known is established as the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject)":
the Master [of the Treatise] relies on the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), wherein there is no conditioned activity and no real existence; whereas the opponent...
According to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is real; however, the principle that the self (*ātman*) is not real is not commonly known to you outsiders.
Therefore, I speak of their distinction. I now establish the statement that it is unreal in order to refute your assertion that it is real.

Therefore, it is said that negating what is not commonly known is established as the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject). It does not arise from that [subject] below. Next, the faults of the reason (*hetu*) are refuted.
That is to say, the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a phenomenon produced through cultivation or volitional construction; this is understood by both our own school and yours.
Therefore, I establish "non-arising" as the reason to prove that the unconditioned is non-existent. Thus, [the section] below concludes its absence.

Regarding the two faults of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*), the opponent objects: "Since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as existent entities do not exist, the reason of 'non-arising,' which depends upon them, is likewise not established.
Now, it is clarified that because both parties agree that unconditioned phenomena are existent entities, the reason of non-arising, which depends upon them, also exists.
Therefore, the conclusion is stated: there are no faults regarding the establishment of the thesis or the reason. Is this not like the case of the "empty flowers" mentioned previously? No.

This refutes the fault of the "unestablished similar example" (*sapakṣāsiddhi*). Regarding the statement that "empty flowers," although they lack a functional entity (*vastu*)—where "entity" (*vastu*) means "substance" (*svabhāva*)—are "the existence of the nature of non-existence of dharmas such as non-arising":
here, "non-arising" is the reason (*hetu*); "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other reasons of the same class;
and the "dharma possessing the subject" (*dharmin*) is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, although these empty flowers lack a substantial reality, they are nonetheless the reason.

The similar instance (sapakṣa) consisting of a real entity that serves as the basis for the property to be proven (sādhyadharma): why is this? Because it lacks substantial reality, being identical to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
By means of this, the meaning of the thesis to be established is successfully proven; thus, there is no fault of the "non-existence of the locus" (āśrayāsiddhi).

This demonstrates the function of citing an example and shows that the example is free from defects. That is to say, by means of a flower in the sky, the reason (hetu) for establishing that thesis is successfully proven.
Because of the meaning of the Dharma, there is no fault of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), the locus (*dharmin*), or the similar example (*sapakṣa*) being unestablished (*asiddha*).

Below the *Vibhāṣā*, next follows the refutation of the sixth position. This text also has two parts: first, the presentation of the opponent's view; second, from the words "This statement... onwards, the Master’s refutation.

Within the former, first is the general negation that it is not so; second, from the words "Cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) onwards, the establishment of the proof by means of formal inference (*prayoga*).
The thesis is that "cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is substantially existent. The reasons are "because it is the object of the Path" and "because it opposes the afflictions.
The phrase "it is not a non-substantial dharma" concludes the establishment of the meaning of its existence. The phrase "this [statement] is merely... is the Master’s refutation;

he states that the expressions "object of the Path" and "opposing the afflictions" only serve to exclude heterogeneous instances (vipakṣa), but lack any illustrative instance (sapakṣa) of a similar class.
Using this to prove that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) exists—how could this argument possibly succeed?

As with the refutation of space (*ākāśa*) below, it is the same as the previous refutation. Below, under the section on space, the refutation of the Vaibhāṣika defense of analytical cessation was already established;
one should not insist upon it again here.
Below the section on the masters of the Sautrāntika school, the seventh position is next refuted. This passage contains two parts: first, the presentation of the external position;

second, from "If this meaning... onwards, the master’s refutation. Regarding the first part, the term "Sautrāntika masters" refers to those who exclusively adhere to the sūtras and do not believe in the Abhidharma.
This position exists among all eighteen schools. What is clarified here specifically concerns the sense faculties (*indriya*).

This master belongs to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school. Within the tenets of this school, it is explained that the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are non-substantial dharmas (*avastuka-dharma*).
Now, the Master of the Treatise states: "The present Master establishes that space is entirely not substantially existent.

Such an inference, if directed against our own school, constitutes the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Below this point, the Master refutes [the opponent's position]. Within this refutation, there are two parts.
First, distinguishing between the two schools’ differing positions: [the opponent’s view] avoids the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Second, following the statement of the thesis to be established, he again cites his own position to demonstrate that both existence and non-existence are refuted. Regarding the former: "I define the essence of space as being in the absence of obstructive matter and so forth;
this is according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), whereby space exists. However, from the perspective of your own school..."

"It is not a case of establishing what is already established; rather, it is because you have analyzed that [space] as being non-existent. This means that within your own school, you have analyzed that space—whether ultimate or conventional—is invariably non-existent.
Thus, immediately following the statement of the thesis, you yourself reiterate your own position to demonstrate that both existence and non-existence are refuted.

It is simply because sentient beings mostly cling to existence that [the teaching] correctly refutes the nature of existence. Once the nature of existence is relinquished, non-existence likewise cannot be established.
For clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence are both extreme views; they do not accord with the principle of the non-duality of existence and non-existence.
Now, the tenet of this treatise transcends the four propositions and eliminates the hundred negations; how, then, could existence or non-existence be apprehended?
Below the section on the Theravāda masters, the eighth misconception is refuted. This passage also consists of two parts: first, an introduction to the external school’s tenet;

second, from "The self-nature of conditioned phenomena" onwards, the Master’s refutation thereof. Within the former, the term "Theravāda" refers to the period one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the time King Aśoka was undermining the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, a younger brother of King Aśoka renounced the world and attained the fruit of an Arhat.
Han-guo (漢果). During the time when the Buddha-dharma was about to perish, he sat in the position of honor.
Fearing that the Buddha-dharma might be further established while no dharma could be obtained, he struck a copper plate with a chisel; thus, the Tripiṭaka masters sent it to the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
Later, King Aśoka, having gained faith in the monks, took the Tripiṭaka from the copper plate and circulated it. It was for this reason that it was so named. This is the aforementioned [text].
The Sthavira school establishes "interstitial matter" (*antarā-rūpa*) and designates it as space (*ākāśa*). Space has two meanings: first, not being obstructed by others;
second, not obstructing others. Although this matter of space does not obstruct others, it is obstructed by earth; therefore, it is called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
As for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) rejected by you, the Master of Treatises, that which exists according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-sat*) is not [identical to] my conditioned [phenomena].

Because they are different, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Regarding the second point, "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth, the Master of the Treatise refutes it by stating:
"Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the conditioned has already been refuted previously, [your position] is likewise untenable. The Master says:

"When I state that space exists, I am speaking of its existence based on conventional designation (*saṃvṛti-prajñapti*); it lacks any fixed nature (*niyata-svabhāva*). Your statement that space exists as form (*rūpa*) refers, however, to a fixed nature."

It exists. Therefore, what I have established does not incur the fault of establishing what is already proven. Furthermore, your adherence to the view that space is material and has the nature of a conditioned phenomenon has already been refuted in the preceding fascicle; thus, it shall not be refuted again here.
Below the section on the Vaibhāṣika masters, the ninth [section] refutes the Vātsīputrīya school, which is the Saṃmitīya school.
Because the tenets accepted by this school are the same as those of the Vaibhāṣikas, it is refuted by referring to them as being identical to the Vaibhāṣikas.

Below the *Saṃprayukta-śāstrins* (Correspondence Theorists), the tenth section refutes the *Yogācārins*. This passage contains two parts: first, the exposition of the tenets established by the Correspondence Theorists;

second, from "In reality, this is not logical" onwards, the Master’s refutation. Within the first [section] regarding their adherence, there are three further divisions. First, the Correspondence Theorists set forth their own position:
"Beyond the ultimate (*paramārtha*), there is no further grasping at a determinate nature as being the ultimate; therefore, it is called the 'ultimate'."

This is the emptiness of meaning (*arthasūnyatā*). Next, it will be clarified that *tathatā* (suchness) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). That is to say, *tathatā* is the ultimate truth of all phenomena;
therefore, *tathatā* is said to be empty from the perspective of the ultimate truth. This means that within *tathatā*, there is no further fixed nature of *tathatā*.
Therefore, it is said that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is empty. Regarding the statement "this accords with principle": this concludes that one's own school [of thought] is correct.

Second, regarding the statement "True Suchness is not substantially existent": this does not accord with principle; the following is not what the Master of the Treatise has established. Third, as for the question "How is it supramundane...": [the response follows].
The principle of self-establishment proves that suchness (*tathatā*) exists.

If one were to claim that suchness is not substantially existent, how could non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) take a non-existent thing as their object? This would contradict the correct principle.
As for subsequently attained wisdom, it arises before and after the true contemplation; because this wisdom of characteristics resembles suchness, it is described in this way.
Regarding the phrase "the two [categories] are not logically tenable," the author of the treatise refutes them. This refutation consists of two parts.

First, the author of the treatise offers a general negation, stating that they are "not logically tenable. This means that the thesis established by you, the Sāṃkhya, is not consistent with correct reasoning.

Second, "As stated below," is the actual refutation. Within this refutation, there are two parts: first, the refutation of the principle of non-discursiveness; second, "Furthermore, as for what you have said below," which refutes their established thesis.

The first part contains three sections: first, the actual refutation; second, citing scriptural statements to establish the proof; third, "Recalling and holding [the opponent's position] below," which restates the point to conclude its invalidity.
Regarding the first of these: "According to what you have said, this non-conceptual wisdom takes non-existent phenomena as its object."

Regarding the point that taking [a non-existent] as an object is not consistent with reason: why is it only the case that taking a non-existent dharma (*abhāva*) as an object is inconsistent with reason?

Taking an existent dharma (*bhāva*) as an object is likewise inconsistent with reason. Although it was stated above that one takes existent and non-existent objects, it was not yet understood which specific dharma constitutes the existent object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Therefore, it is now said: it is not by apprehending *tathatā* (suchness) as truly existent that one attains consistency with reason.
Because it is difficult to establish that the apprehension of *tathatā* (suchness) as having a real, intrinsic nature [is valid], this section specifically refutes its existence as a nature.

This is because it is unreasonable for one to know for oneself that a non-existent dharma serves as an object of cognition; thus, there is a specific refutation regarding the fault of [asserting] existence.
Why? Because it is difficult to establish. The wisdom that takes *tathatā* as its object is not the truly supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); this is...
The thesis is established: "Because it has an object of cognition," and so forth. The reason is established as follows:

if there were an external object of cognition for a cognition, that would be a conceptualizing cognition, not non-conceptualizing wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it is conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*):

in non-conceptualizing wisdom, the wisdom and its object are equal and identical; one cannot speak of a distinction such as being conditioned. If there were an object of cognition external to that wisdom, then...

Seeing that cognition (*jñāna*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while its object (*viṣaya*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is itself a discriminative cognition; therefore, it is said to "pertain to the conditioned.
Such a cognition that takes [the unconditioned] as its object is a case of an analogy based on a causal factor (*hetu-dharma*).

Thus, this cognition that arises simultaneously with a conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and takes an object has an objective referent external to the cognition itself. Since it is a conditioned, discriminative cognition, this [cognition] which takes...
If the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) also has an object of cognition (*ālambana*), why should it alone not be a conditioned, conceptual wisdom?

For this reason, the passage beginning with "Thus the sutra says" cites four scriptural passages to prove that non-conceptual wisdom has no object of cognition. The first sutra passage proves that there is no such object as the realm of *tathatā*.
The second sutra passage proves that because the wisdom does not even function, it is free from names and words; [the wisdom] does not even...
The practice reveals that wisdom does not exist, let alone names and designations; it reveals that objects do not exist. This is what is meant by the equality of object and wisdom.
The third sutra proves that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is not that which performs a direct realization (*abhisamaya*); it reveals that wisdom is not a subject that takes an object.

*Bodhi* is translated here as "wisdom" (*jñāna*), and is also called "awakening" (*bodha*). The fourth sutra further proves that the meaning of the "object of cognition" is supreme: the realm of the truths (*satya*) does not exist. Because...

Because True Suchness (tathatā) is an object of cognition (ālambana), he again cites a sūtra to prove its non-existence. Third, from "If one can remember and maintain this" onwards, he restates the point to conclude that it is incorrect.

This section contains two parts: first, restating the point to conclude that it is incorrect; second, from "Furthermore, regarding that True Suchness," establishing a formal argument (pramāṇa) to refute it.
Regarding the first part: if you were able to remember and maintain these four sūtras, you should not admit that this [True Suchness] is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa).

Wisdom is that which can effect clear realization (*abhisamaya*). This [proponent] maintains that this wisdom is not a cognitive subject (*ālambaka*), and that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not its objective referent (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, regarding that True Suchness, he establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to negate it, stating: "That True Suchness is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)."
This is the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Because it is an object of cognition" is the reason (*hetu*). "Just like form and so forth" is the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

For instance, the five sense objects such as form, and a portion of the mental object (*dharma-āyatana*), are not ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) because they are objects of cognition; true suchness (*tathatā*) is likewise so.
Since it is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), how can it alone be the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?

Having thus concluded the refutation of their non-logical position above, the following section secondly refutes their established thesis. This passage contains three parts; first, it restates their prior view, hence the word "Furthermore" (*punar*).
Regarding your statement that "there is no further ultimate truth beyond the ultimate truth," and so forth: following these words, you state your own position.

That is to say, just as you establish [the emptiness] of the Teacher and others in relation to their conceptual designations (*saṃjñā*), if one considers this ultimate suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "empty" because this suchness lacks any such determinate nature (*niyata-svabhāva*).
Below the section on "various silken garments," the text clearly sets forth the refutation. Within this refutation, there are four parts: first, the refutation by establishing a logical principle;

second, from "as it is said" onwards, the refutation by citing scriptural testimony; third, from "if one says 'the true nature'" onwards, the refutation of their attempted defense; and fourth, from "having fully ceased the extensive dispute" onwards, the cessation of the dispute and the pointing toward the teaching.
Regarding the first part, the refutation by establishing a logical principle, there are three sections. The first is the refutation by raising an instance to demand consistency: "You..."
If it were claimed that one who perceives no further ultimate truth upon the ultimate truth is called a "seer of reality," then even cowherds and the like—
who do not perceive any further heavy garments or silk upon their clothes and silks—
would also be called "seers of reality," because the emptiness observed in both cases is identical. Second, the following clarifies this point:
This is a refutation of groundless objections. Furthermore, such emptiness is taught as an antidote to various wrong views.
That is to say, if you claim that within the ultimate there exists another ultimately existent intrinsic nature, you are called a person of wrong view.

The Buddha taught the emptiness of the ultimate as an antidote for such people of wrong view. This [passage] restates their position; regarding the ultimate, above and below, the Master of the Treatise...
Refutation: This refers to the view that, upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there exists yet another determinate nature of the ultimate. Such a wicked person has never existed in the world;

therefore, one should not refute his assertion by stating that the ultimate is empty. Third, from "Furthermore, that... onwards, it clarifies the refutation through contradiction with inference (*anumāna*).

Furthermore, that *tathatā* (suchness) is free from the natures of existence and non-existence; it is neither the subject that cognizes nor the object that is cognized. When realized by wisdom, it is equanimous.

[These are] equal and impartial. You now, however, maintain that *tathatā* (suchness) exists as the object of cognition (*ālambana*), and that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*).
You merely state that upon *tathatā*, one should not again perceive *tathatā*; therefore, you name it "emptiness of *tathatā*" (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).
Thus, the reasoning that asserts *tathatā* (suchness) as having an intrinsic nature has already been refuted by me,

as previously stated, through the logic of inference (*anumāna*)— namely, that unconditioned phenomena lack reality because they do not arise, being comparable to flowers in the sky; it should not be established further.

The second section, "As Stated Below," cites scriptural passages to provide proof and refute [the opponent's position]. This section contains four parts: 1. It clarifies that the Tathāgata does not perceive either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Nirvāṇa is precisely suchness (tathatā). If suchness were an entity possessing a real intrinsic nature, why would the Tathāgata say it is identical to the false and illusory saṃsāra, and further state that he perceives neither?
2. From "Having already correctly realized wisdom" onwards, it distinguishes [the state of] non-... [text truncated]

The reason for this vision is as follows: because the Tathāgata has correctly and fully realized that there are no afflictions arising from inversion, and that these very afflictions arising from inversion are, by their very nature, ultimately devoid of any self-nature of arising—it is this that is called *nirvāṇa*.
What, then, could there be to be seen? Third, from "In this way" onwards, the characteristics of the realization through wisdom are explained. This is the section.

A distinct cognition. It is not a "correct cognition" (samyag-jñāna) because it correctly cognizes that the intrinsic nature of *nirvāṇa* is ultimately [non-existent], for cognition lacks intrinsic nature.

Nor is it an "incorrect cognition," because it is a cognition by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). For this reason, it is called "conventionally designated non-conceptual wisdom" (*prajñapti-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Furthermore, it may be said to be neither knowing nor not-knowing; thus it is called "conventionally designated non-conceptual wisdom. 4. From here on, [the text] explains based on this sacred teaching.

The sūtra reveals the characteristic of detachment. This passage consists of four parts: First, based on this sacred teaching, one should know that *nirvāṇa-tathatā* (the suchness of nirvāṇa) is simply the eternal cessation of all conceptual construction;

it is not a non-existent entity, nor does it possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Second, "not apart from" and so forth: this is an analytical explanation revealing that *nirvāṇa* is without [intrinsic] nature.
That is to say, it is not characterized by a transformational basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) that is apart from *tathatā*, which lacks a real intrinsic nature. Thus, the *dharmakāya* is established.

This refers to the statement that the *dharmakāya* is itself *nirvāṇa*. Third, from "by attaining" (*yasmāt prāpti*) downwards, the text follows the explanation to reveal that the *dharmakāya* is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Regarding "by attaining the true path of antidote which is the contemplation of emptiness": this refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is metaphorically designated as the "true path of antidote.

Regarding "all conceptualization" (*sarva-vikalpa*) and so forth, it sets forth that which is to be remedied; since it is ultimately without intrinsic nature, it is metaphorically designated as the "transformed basis," the *dharmakāya*.
It can be understood according to the text. Fourth, "As stated in the Sūtra" and below, citations are introduced to establish the proof; this text can also be understood.
Third, "If one says that the true [nature] is as follows" and below, the refutation of the corresponding teacher’s defense; the text has two parts: first, restating his defensive argument.
The second section, "Furthermore, the non-Buddhists below," extensively refutes the counter-arguments. Within the first part, the *Sāṃkhyas* (Correspondence Masters) offer this defense:
"In the sutras, it is stated that even wisdom does not function, much less names and designations;

and in this context, the passage regarding 'no dharma being visible' and so forth is spoken because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is free from characteristics and free from verbal expression. It does not mean that True Suchness is ultimately non-existent."

Having made this statement, the Master of the Treatise now cites their defensive argument, saying: "If you say that although *tathatā* (suchness) is beyond verbal expression, it is substantially existent...
From "as for the two" down to "the non-Buddhists," there is a detailed refutation of the defense in four parts.

First, it clarifies that the names and characteristics of *tathatā* and the *ātman* (self) are difficult to distinguish and that their essence is no different; thus, this *tathatā* of yours is identical to that of the non-Buddhists...
As for the concept of the self (*ātman*), its essence is no different; it is merely that the mind conceptualizes distinctions through names and characteristics.

What you call *tathatā* (suchness), non-Buddhists call the self; there is no difference in their essence. As in the passage concerning "the two suchnesses," the two characteristics of *tathatā* and the self are extensively analyzed.
In the text, the characteristic of *tathatā* is first analyzed: although this *tathatā* is substantially existent, [it is so].

Regarding the essence of suchness within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it cannot be conceptually grasped through the linguistic and mental activities associated with attributes such as existence or non-existence, as it is not identical to objects such as form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, conceptual constructions such as "existence" or "non-existence" are not established.
I shall likewise proceed as follows. Next, the characteristics of the self (*ātman*) are analyzed. This section consists of three parts:

first, the analysis of the essence of the self, which is substantially existent, all-pervading throughout the *dharmadhātu*, eternally abiding and unchanging, capable both of acting and of experiencing. Second, from "yet it is free from conceptual construction" (*vibhāga-vinirmukta*) onwards, the isolation of the essence of the self is revealed.

First, the characteristic of being free [from conceptualization] is indicated in general; thus it says, "yet it is free from conceptual construction. This explains the characteristic of being free [from conceptualization].
Therefore, it is said that "it is not within the range of verbal expression," which means that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity has ceased.

Thus, it is called "free from conceptual discrimination. Below this, the section on "summarizing the freedom from characteristics" is clear. Third, the section beginning with "In that teaching... cites scriptural statements to provide proof; this is easily understood.

Third, the section beginning with "Since the mark of self is thus... raises a comparison to challenge the difference; it contains two parts: first, challenging the difference by means of the same [principle]; second...
What is the distinction here? This concludes the summary that equates the general critique with the specific one. Regarding the first part:

since the essence and characteristics of the self (*ātman*) exist, pervading the *dharmadhātu*, eternally abiding, and free from marks—thus being no different from *tathatā*—it is said that while the characteristic of the self is thus, you further claim that liberation is attained by wisdom taking *tathatā* as its object, and not by wisdom taking the self as its object. What is the distinction between these two?

"Below: 'Concluding by equating the collective and distinguishing the individual'—the textual structure is easily understood. Fourth, 'Only clinging to factions'—below this, it clarifies that the Dharma is identical while the sentiments are divided, manifesting one's own lack of faith.

This means: 'Your associated teachers exclusively form factions and claim that wisdom attains liberation by taking True Suchness (tathatā) as its object, whereas it cannot attain [liberation] by taking a self (ātman) as its object.
Non-Buddhists are likewise; they exclusively form factions and claim that wisdom [attains liberation] by taking a self as its object."
One can attain liberation; it cannot be attained by taking True Suchness (tathatā) as a causal condition. Therefore, I have concluded below that [your teaching] is not to be believed. This means:

"The True Suchness conceived by you, the Master of Correspondence, is similar to that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika); therefore, I cannot accept it with faith. The phrase "truly existent yet not existent" further clarifies the point of similarity:
both parties reckon it to be existent, yet both also reckon it to be non-existent; both likewise maintain that it is free from characteristics.
Therefore, it is said that they do not exist.

Regarding the section "Fourth, furthermore, extensively debating below," this serves to quell debate and cease further discourse. Regarding the section "Those who are weary of and terrified by existence below," this explains the intended meaning of the words; the textual structure is clear and can be understood.

Furthermore, there is a section concerning those of the same class who ride inferior vehicles, which refutes the eleventh misconception. This passage consists of four parts: first, the presentation of the externalist's position;
second, the master’s refutation beginning with "If [the Buddha] does not reveal..."; third, the externalist's defense beginning with "If [he] does not speak..."; and fourth, the conclusion.

Regarding the statement below that "the four [aggregates] truly exist," the Master of the Treatise provides an explanation to resolve this. The preceding section has two parts. First, he cites the fact that their locus is identical as proof that they must possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

That is to say, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) collectively subsume both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; since conditioned phenomena already possess an intrinsic nature, [it follows that the others do as well].

Therefore, we know that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) also definitely possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, it is said that the twelve bases (*āyatana*) encompass both the conditioned and the unconditioned, and that they definitely possess their own intrinsic nature.

Second, because [the unconditioned] such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth can all serve as objects (*viṣaya*), giving rise to the Path and extinguishing evil, this proves that they definitely possess an intrinsic nature.
That is to say, these twelve bases are precisely the objects of the Four Noble Truths; by contemplating these four objects, the sixteen aspects of wisdom (*ṣoḍaśākārajñāna*) are produced.
The passage below explains that by diligently cultivating [the path] based on these four objects, one is able to extinguish afflictions and cease suffering.

If the unconditioned were identical to space—devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva)—how could it function as an object in the same way as conditioned phenomena to give rise to the Path and eliminate evil?
Since it can indeed give rise to the Path and eliminate evil, we know for certain that it possesses intrinsic nature. The meaning of the text is clear.
Second, "If one does not reveal [this]" and below, the Master of the Treatise refutes [the opponent]. Within this refutation, there are three parts. First:
If one cannot know that the nature of all phenomena is empty, then for all noble beings (ārya), there would be no principle of abandoning evil and advancing toward good.

This means that if the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena were not revealed, sentient beings would all claim that all phenomena and suffering possess a fixed nature (*svabhāva*). If the nature were fixed...
There is [no one who could do so]. Who would be able to abandon the afflictions, sufferings, and faults of the three realms?
If the nature of all virtuous merits were fixed, who would be able to cultivate meritorious dharmas and achieve progress?

Furthermore, even if the two or three vehicles were inferior, if their wisdom could not know that the nature of all phenomena is empty, there would be no distinction between the noble paths of the three vehicles; for they would not be performing the cultivation of dharmas.

Regarding the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*): since one performs only the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), there can be no distinction in the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
There may only be distinctions in the provisions (*sambhāra*), faculties (*indriya*), and dispositions (*adhimukti*). Third, regarding "all those below":

if one cannot know that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is empty, there would be no distinction among the liberations of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). This passage contains two parts; the first clarifies the performance of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons.

Because of the removal of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one attains the liberation of the Two Vehicles. This passage consists of two parts: first, resolving the objection raised by the opponent; the objection states:
"All that I have cited above are the words of the Buddha; do you, the master of the treatise, not believe them? Second, the master of the treatise replies: [as follows].

I accept and uphold all of this. This is because the Buddha, wishing to have people of the present rely upon worldly conventions, employed the principle of "truth" (satya) to distinguish between different modes of observation;
however, this serves only to suppress afflictions and is not their ultimate eradication.

Furthermore, it reveals that the liberation through the realization of the emptiness of persons attained by the two vehicles has not yet reached the ultimate, as it is entirely lost within the Noble Vehicle of the Buddhas. Therefore, it is called the "worldly principle" (*saṃvṛti-yukti*). Relying upon this—
The conventional truth explains the distinctions between the paths of those two vehicles; it does not refer to distinctions in the ultimate principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

If one departs from the lower [levels], it clarifies that by practicing the contemplation of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma-śūnyatā*), one attains the liberation of the Buddha Vehicle. However, the text provides an inverse explanation, which can be understood according to the literal phrasing.
If explained in its proper order, it should state: because the Buddha has realized and entered the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), he is able to effect eternal severance.
Because of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the Great Master [attains] ultimate liberation.

that is, from the perspective of the meaning that all three vehicles are identical in their liberation from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), [the sūtra] was thus composed.

This explanation—stating that "the two are not all" and so forth—interprets the meaning behind the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles regarding liberation as expressed in the scriptures.

Specifically, when the sūtras state that the three vehicles sit together upon the bed of liberation without distinction, this is said on the basis that the three vehicles are identical in their liberation from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and thus not different in that regard.
It does not mean that they are identical in their knowledge of the distinct categories of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).

Their intrinsic nature is entirely empty. Because they are liberated from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is said thus. This is the explanation by way of the Dharma. To explain by means of an analogy:

the two liberations differ in their degree of excellence. For example, the space within a pore and the great void of the sky—though their emptiness is the same, there is no lack of distinction between their magnitude.
When liberation through the emptiness of persons is compared to liberation through the emptiness of phenomena...
It is likewise so. Although emptiness is the same, there is no lack of distinction between its shallow and deep aspects.

If it were otherwise—as explained below by way of refutation—that the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas were indistinguishable from the Buddha-vehicle (Buddhayāna) regarding the depth of their realization of emptiness, then the Buddhas would be unable to manifest the activity of superior fruition, and what they have realized would not be ultimate. Let us now conclude this digression.

Regarding the "Discernment of the Correct Doctrine" (*Bianzheng lun*): it exhorts one to cease extensive disputes. Herein, the "correct doctrine" refers to discerning whether the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena exists or does not exist.

The "incidental doctrine" refers to clarifying the superiority or inferiority of various forms of liberation. Since the superiority or inferiority of liberation is not what is being primarily clarified here, it is advised that this matter be set aside for now.
As for the fixed nature of all phenomena, its elucidation is not yet complete; therefore, it must be discerned.

Second, regarding the cultivation of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-caryā*) below: next, there is the specific refutation of the attachments of various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Within this section, there are two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent;
second, from "this intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) onwards, the actual refutation of their calculations.

The three realms likewise transform from empty flowers; the three realms also take self-nature as their substance. Since empty flowers take self-nature as their substance, these empty flowers are dharmas that possess a substance.

Second, this is inferior because it refutes the proponent’s *sapakṣa* (similar instance) and *dṛṣṭānta* (example), thereby demonstrating that the proponent’s thesis (*pakṣa*) is unestablished.
Now, for a similar instance in a formal argument, it must be accepted by both parties. Since my own position asserts that a sky-flower exists, the proponent would have no similar instance.
If there is no similar instance, the thesis being established—that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack substantial reality—is also unestablished. Therefore, it is said:
Because that [position] exists, the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is unestablished, as it contradicts what is being established (*sādhya*). Second, "Now one should interrogate...

Therefore, you contradict and undermine your own school’s tenet regarding emptiness. That the three realms and the flowers in the sky are distinct entities is what the world at large accepts.
[It is] known. Now, it is said that the three realms are themselves like flowers in the sky; therefore, it is said that [the opponent's position] contradicts what is commonly known.
If one were to say that the three realms are not like flowers in the sky, this would be a restatement of the subsequent question. This would constitute the fault of [the opponent’s] own composition:

namely, since the three realms are not like flowers in the sky, then flowers in the sky would not be the same as the three realms, and the three realms would have [some other] thing as their essence. This being so—
Since the self-nature of a flower in the sky is definitively empty and non-existent, it is said that "this is indeed non-existent.

Since the flower in the sky lacks intrinsic nature, the concordant example I have established is proven. Once the point that the flower in the sky has no reality is established, you lose your own fundamental thesis that the flower exists.

Suffering, pleasure, delusion, and so forth, are the distinctions of its names. "The second" refers to the various lower [views]. The opponent establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) to prove existence;

That is to say, "the fact that manifest phenomena possess an intrinsic nature" is the reason (*hetu*). This constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Manifest phenomena" are the subject (*dharmin*), referring to the five [aggregates] such as the great grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
There are only the five aggregates, the four elements, and the faculties; these twenty phenomena appear and are visible, and are therefore called manifest entities (*dṛśya-vastu*).
Existence (*sattā*) is their cause; this is the property (*dharma*), meaning that each of the aforementioned manifest entities has its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) acting as the cause.

This property and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*) are inseparable, which constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Because there are types" is the reason (*hetu*) for establishing [the thesis]; that is, by means of the intrinsic nature...
Because of their genus (*jāti*). All things that possess a genus are seen to have existence as their cause, just like a piece of sandalwood.

This is an analogy based on commonality (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): for example, if one *liǎng* of sandalwood is divided into many pieces, the fragrance within all those pieces remains exactly as it was originally.
The manifestation of phenomena is likewise: although they may transform into twenty-three different types, within each type, they remain identical to their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, below the section on "manifest phenomena" (*dṛśya-vastu*), the person (*puruṣa*) is established as the valid cognizer (*pramāṇa*) to prove that the person exists.
To say "these manifest phenomena have an experiencer" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Manifest phenomena consist of twenty-three factors; these are the subject (*dharmin*).

"Having an experiencer" refers to the self (*ātman*); this is the predicate (*dharma*). The inseparability of the predicate and the subject is called the thesis, because it is that which is to be experienced.

This is the reason: it demonstrates that the manifest object (*vastu*) is what is experienced and enjoyed by the person (*puruṣa*). Regarding the phrase "all that is experienced and enjoyed," the following provides a formal analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) which is easy to understand.
