This is the aspect of practice (*ākāra*). Regarding the initial teaching on the Dharma in the section on the text: the statement "to eliminate coarse characteristics" means that, within this context, it eliminates the obstacle of having characteristics (*sanimitta-āvaraṇa*);

compared to the subsequent elimination of the obstacle of signlessness (*animitta-āvaraṇa*), this is described as "coarse. The second part, beginning with "like a physician treating blurred vision," is a metaphorical explanation that is easy to understand.

Within this section, the second part clarifies the elimination of the obstacle of signlessness (*animitta*) and reveals wisdom. This textual division consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the obstacle of signlessness.

It says: "Although within this category one has already attained non-abiding"—this means that although within this category of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena characterized by signs, one has already attained the practice of non-abiding in signs and does not cling to their existence.

Although [the practitioner] abides in the continuous flow of mental application through the active manifestation of conceptualizations such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they have not yet attained immovability.
This refers to one who understands that the active manifestation of conceptualizations regarding emptiness and so forth obstructs supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

That is to say, while contemplating the signlessness (*animitta*) of objects can indeed dismantle objects characterized by signs (*nimitta*), this very conceptualization of an object as "signless"—if it...

One engages in the manifestation of the discrimination of signlessness. Since this mind of signlessness is still a state of effortful application, it continues to persist and further becomes an obstacle to emptiness.
Moreover, this obstacle to emptiness can also obstruct the immovable and non-conceptual wisdom.

If one has not yet attained this immovable and non-conceptual wisdom, there is no means by which one could understand that the manifestation of the discrimination of emptiness and so forth can act as [an obstacle].

Obstruction. This refers to the obstruction of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). The second [verse], beginning with "desiring to abandon the lower," presents the counter-obstacle (*pratipakṣa*) as wisdom;
it reveals that wisdom is capable of extinguishing obstructions. The phrase "desiring to abandon" clarifies the purpose of cultivating wisdom:

it means that because one desires to abandon the obstruction of signlessness (*animitta*), one must contemplate all phenomena as both existent and non-existent, and thereby abandon them. However, one cultivates the counter-obstacle...
One must not treat this treatment with laxity; therefore, it is said: "With courageous and correct diligence, one observes in this way. Regarding the phrase "observes in this way":
within the context of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), even the object of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not truly existent. This is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The word "etcetera" includes existence, both existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and so forth. That is to say, within the category of ultimate truth:

There are no such four attachments. "Because they arise from conditions" is the stated reason (*hetu*). "Like illusions and so forth" is the illustrative example based on commonality (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Since illusions and the like arise from conditions and are not substantially real, the objects of the four attachments—emptiness and so forth—likewise arise from conditions.
How could they be substantially existent? Regarding this, the third [section] should clarify the benefit; since the benefit is no different from what was stated previously, it is not mentioned here.
The same applies to the following two.

Third, regarding the diligent cultivation below, there is the obstacle of both existence and non-existence. This passage contains three parts. First, it first raises the obstacle of the characteristic of both existence and non-existence.

The statement, "By thus diligently cultivating, one is further able to eliminate the conceptualization of emptiness as both existent and non-existent," means that I previously relied upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to thus diligently cultivate, and was further able to eliminate the conceptualization of emptiness as both existent and non-existent.

This is the obstruction of the objective aspect of non-equal conceptualization. Initially, there is the sickness of existence; one diligently cultivates emptiness to extinguish this sickness of existence.

Although emptiness is discarded once the sickness is removed, it may itself become a sickness again. However, regarding the sickness of fixed determination, one must not exclusively adopt the removal of existence, because existence is already a sickness in its own right.
For this reason, when the sicknesses of both existence and emptiness arise, one must further diligently cultivate both existence and non-existence. And...
One dispels the illness of emptiness. Although the illness of emptiness is extinguished, the state of being both existent and non-existent again becomes an illness.
However, this illness of being both existent and non-existent cannot be eliminated unless one diligently cultivates the contemplation of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Therefore, it is now said that by thus diligently cultivating the contemplation of ultimate truth, one is not only able to eliminate the illness of emptiness, but is also able to eliminate the state of being both existent and non-existent.

This is the affliction of non-conceptualization. "Emptiness" refers to the affliction of emptiness itself. "And so forth" includes the afflictions of both existence and non-existence, as well as neither existence nor non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "second, because of eliminating those": this refers to citing the wisdom in contrast to the obstacles to demonstrate that wisdom can extinguish those obstacles.
"Because of eliminating those" means eliminating the afflictions of existence, non-existence, and both existence and non-existence. Emptiness.
"Being free from the two extremes of non-emptiness and so forth, one never again observes phenomena through the aspects of emptiness and so forth.
Regarding the "two extremes," this refers to the two extremes of existence and non-existence. This clarifies that wisdom can extinguish hindrances so that they do not arise.

The third section, "as explained below," provides a specific exposition on the establishment of realization. Initially, eight pairs are established in relation to the five aggregates. [The first pair is] signlessness (*animitta*).

Contemplating the first four pairs constitutes the eight gates of cultivation. The latter three constitute the three gates of emptiness. The eighth [pair] summarizes the characteristics of contemplation.
Just as the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the object of contemplation, so too are the other four aggregates, such as sensation (*vedanā*).

Subsequently, this is extended by analogy to the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).

Samādhi and dhāraṇī-gates, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). This means that regarding these various dharma-gates, one fears not contemplating them as permanent, and so forth, up to not contemplating them as being free from attachment; hence it says "and so forth," and the text is all intelligible.
Fourth, "Since one can thus distance oneself from the two extremes," and so forth, [this section] eliminates the obstacle of the characteristics of neither existence nor non-existence.
Within this passage there are three parts. First, it first presents the obstacle regarding the objective characteristics of neither existence nor non-existence:

"Since one can thus distance oneself from the two extremes"—that is, the two extremes of both existence and non-existence—one is then able to cultivate the sublime practice that abides in the middle way. This means:
Because it is obstructed by the preceding [notion] of both existence and non-existence, the characteristic of being neither existent nor non-existent arises.

This negation of the characteristics of neither existence nor non-existence is taught as the Middle Way and the Sublime because it counters the obstruction of the preceding characteristic of both existence and non-existence;

for that [preceding view] is an extreme and is coarse. Second, regarding the phrase "this is free from the two extremes" and below: this sets forth wisdom in contrast to the obstructions to manifest it.

Wisdom is able to extinguish obstacles. It is said that this abiding in the Middle Way, free from the two extremes, is due to the two kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—the conditioned and the unconditioned—as explained above.

This means that this principle of the sublime practice of the Middle Way, which remains far removed from the two extremes, serves as the antidote for extinguishing the obstacles of "neither existence nor non-existence. Nevertheless, regarding the objects of the conditioned and the unconditioned...
To perceive existence as being neither existent nor non-existent does not accord with the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Therefore, know that I have previously relied upon the principle of ultimate truth to set forth two types of inference: "In their true nature, conditioned phenomena are empty, because they arise dependently like illusions."
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has no reality; its non-arising is like a flower in the sky. This is because the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) transcends these four truths.

Without the realization of ultimate wisdom, there is no means by which [afflictions] can be extinguished. By citing the meaning of the aforementioned inference, it is shown that realized wisdom is the remedy for this obstacle.
Since teaching arises based on realization, the teaching is cited here to manifest the realization. Because the category of form (*rūpa*) does not exist...

Below, the characteristics of the sublime practice (mārga-caryā) situated in the middle are extensively distinguished. That is to say, regarding conditioned and unconditioned phenomena such as the categories of form and so forth, there are six aspects:
being formless, non-demonstrable, non-abiding, non-manifesting, non-conceptualizable, and signless. When one realizes the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), object and wisdom are equal;
how could there be any aspect of practice to be apprehended? Here, by citing the intention behind the notion of "sublime practice," the excellence [of this realization] is revealed.
It is signless (*animitta*). To explain these six signlessnesses, the text consists of six sections, which can be understood accordingly.
From the third section, "As the World-Honored One [taught] below," citations are introduced to establish the proof of the six practices of signlessness.

Up to this point, it has been clarified that at the time of the superior cultivation of wisdom, regarding all objects—whether conditioned or unconditioned—one does not grasp at signs or signlessness, nor at both.
It is signless; it is neither characterized by existence nor non-existence. This means it is able to extinguish the obstacles of the four types of false attachment regarding perceived objects.
This clarifies non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which does not perceive an objective referent.

From here below is the second section, which clarifies that since one is thus able [to know], there is no perception of non-existence regarding the objects of knowledge, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This clarifies that the cognizing wisdom (*ālambaka-jñāna*) is not perceived; this is the equality of object and wisdom, because there is neither a cognizer nor an object of cognition.
This is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). What is called "sage-wisdom" (*ārya-jñāna*) is not without a tenet. "Without a tenet" means without...

Regarding the characteristics: the empty mind is not without resonance; yet he who resonates has no mind. This is what is meant by the mutual merging of inner and outer, where both object and contemplation are stilled.
Within this passage there are four points: namely, when one is about to enter the realization of this non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), first one must recognize the obstacles;
second, one must recognize the remedies; third, through recognizing the obstacles, the obstacles themselves cease; fourth...

Because one understands the antidotes, one is able to enter into realization. Regarding the first [point] among the aforementioned, which concerns the necessity of identifying the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), there are two types of obstacles:
first, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the perceived object (*grāhya*). One must thoroughly understand that this obstructs non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*);

since the former has already been clarified as being abandoned, it is said: "If one can thus distance oneself from these two... Although the actual [obstacles] are four, they are referred to as "two" because...
These four extremes originally consist only of existence and non-existence; thus, they are explained by way of their basis, and are therefore called the "two extremes.

Here, "two" refers to the two aspects that can eliminate [the extremes], while the four [extremes] refer to the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) which is designated as "perception" (*saṃjñā*). Now, when it says "the perception of non-duality," this refers to the object-aspect of the focal object mentioned above;

"two" is spoken of here by way of its basis. Now, in clarifying the perception of the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that eliminates [the extremes], "two" is likewise spoken of by way of its basis.

Therefore, it is said that while abiding in the state of non-dual perception, one gives rise to the conceptualization of the aspect of non-duality; furthermore, one is able to recognize that this is an obstacle to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The preceding section concludes the clarification of the two obstacles regarding the aspects and the perceiving subject of consciousness.

As for the phrase "peacefully abiding," this single clause clarifies the antidote that recognizes [the nature of] consciousness. If one perceives the aspect of an apprehended object (*grāhya*) as well as the apprehending wisdom (*grāhaka*), [one must apply the remedy].

Consequently, conceptual discrimination becomes turbulent and restless, and there is no way for it to be stilled. Therefore, one must rely on the object and wisdom of tranquility and abide in equanimity;

only then can one realize the non-dual, non-conceptual wisdom of the non-duality of object and wisdom. Third, following the explanation of the causes below, this addresses the aforementioned obstacle of consciousness.
The fault ceases. Regarding the statement that "the causes as previously described can be swiftly and permanently severed":

as explained above, the cognition that perceives objects is itself the cause of conceptualization. Once this cause is permanently eliminated, both conceptual speech and conceptual mental discourse are entirely stilled.
Fourth, regarding "attainment," it corresponds to the aforementioned remedy for consciousness. Thus...

Because one is able to enter and realize it, it is said that one realizes the true nature of all phenomena—which is immovable, non-manifesting, signless, and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Regarding its objects of focus, one enters into realization without movement, abiding in a continuous stream of sublime knowledge of its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

These ten phrases distinguish the characteristics of the realization of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*): the first five state the characteristics, while the latter five provide their explanation. As for the term "realization" (*prāpti*):
"Immovable" means that because one has realized the signless (*animitta*) regarding its object of focus, it is not moved by the aspect of signs (*nimittabhāga*).
"Without manifestation" means that when non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) correctly enters into realization, there is no manifesting aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of a cognizing wisdom.
"Signless" means that at the time of the correct realization of non-conceptual wisdom, one realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Principle has no dualistic self-characteristics; it does not refer to the realization of a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, there is no objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of an object to be realized.

Regarding the phrase "free from all conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*): the various non-conceptual wisdoms (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) are the truly sublime wisdom that remains far removed from all conceptual proliferation and discrimination.
Regarding "the true nature of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*): this refers to non-conceptual wisdom ceasing [discursive thought] and realizing the true nature of all phenomena.
At the time of its nature, it abides in continuity; object and wisdom are equal, with nothing to be grasped or rejected.
Thus far, the extensive explanation of the superior cultivation of wisdom that realizes non-conceptual gnosis is concluded.
Although one diligently practices [the preceding], the second section clarifies the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as the basis for non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Wisdom that merely severs delusions must rely upon concentration to be able to eliminate them; therefore, after explaining wisdom, the concentration that serves as its basis is explained next.

This passage contains two parts: first, it clarifies the concentration that is the very basis of wisdom; second, from "As the World-Honored One said... onwards, it cites scriptural authority to establish this point. Regarding the first part:

At the beginning and middle [of the practice], although one diligently cultivates the non-erroneous contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), this is characterized by the realization of wisdom (*prajñā*) through subsequent observation.

This is precisely observing that there is nothing to be observed; yet, regarding the nature of emptiness, one ultimately does not effect a realization. Emptiness is characterized by the absence of realization through observation;

this is precisely the cessation (*śamatha*) of that which is to be ceased. These two factors of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are simultaneous within a single moment of thought; thus, the "two absences" are taught.

The two characteristics. Unlike other types of concentration involving discernment and wisdom, although these two are simultaneous and both are counted as "two," they possess two distinct characteristics.
This is what is called "meditative absorption in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha-dhyāna*). This concludes the clarification that this concentration is the true, supreme meditative absorption.

As the Blessed One said in the passage beginning with "Although one cultivates meditative absorption," he provides scriptural citations to establish this proof, namely: "not relying on the five aggregates," "the ten [bases]," and "the twelve [bases]."
The locations, the body and mind, the four great elements, and so forth—their textual passages are intelligible.
Below the section on the *Saṃprayukta-śāstra* masters, the third part clarifies how wisdom differs according to various schools, exhorting beings to adopt or reject [their views].

Within this section, there are two parts. First, it introduces the differing schools, namely the proponents of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* within the Mahāyāna, who assert that [consciousness] is without parts (*nirbhāga*).
Regarding "distinctive wisdom": it is said that there is a fixed attachment to the claim that all conceptualizations of the grasped and the grasper are entirely transcended;
this is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom. To then give rise to a notion of substantiality within that very state and to apply oneself with effort to its cultivation—[this is an error].

This refers to the time when one correctly realizes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). At that time, one is far removed from the apprehended aspect (*grāhya-bhāga*) as well as the subjective aspects of the seer and the seen (*grāhaka-dṛśya-bhāga*).
This wisdom capable of being free from these two aspects is called non-conceptual wisdom.
One then takes this very wisdom—which has forgotten both the apprehended and the apprehender—to be the true characteristic of non-conceptual wisdom and diligently practices it. [Question: ...

If non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) does not grasp the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), then there would have to be a phenomenon external to consciousness that serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for that non-conceptual wisdom;
in that case, the principle that all phenomena are "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) would not be established. The Master of Yoga (*yogācārya*) provides the answer:

because it takes the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness itself as its object-condition, it is established as consciousness-only; it is not the case that there is a separate phenomenon external to consciousness serving as its object.
This is the causal condition (*pratyaya*).
Second, there is a further section below this that explains its refutation. Within the refutation, there are two parts: first, a general refutation of the object of cognition;

second, from the words "furthermore, examining... onwards, a specific refutation of the essence of cognition. Within the former, there are again three sections; first, establishing an inference (*anumāna*) to provide a general refutation.

1. Regarding the object of cognition (*jñeya-viṣaya*). Below this, the sūtra is cited as scriptural proof. 2. From "By this principle and teaching" onwards, the refutation of fixed attachments is concluded.

Within the preceding formal argument (*pramāṇa*), there are two parts: first, establishing two types of valid cognition to refute the object of cognition; second, citing the reasons for these two types of valid cognition.
Next, the object of knowledge is refuted as not being supreme. First, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established: "Such a cognition arises;
although there is no conceptualization as described above"—this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The phrase "such a cognition arises" refers to the arising of a cognition that is devoid of differentiation.
This is the subject (*dharmin*). "Although there is no conceptualization as described above" means that although there is no [conceptualization] as described above...
It is said that the two aspects of the grasped and the grasper—the objective and subjective divisions—are conventionally described as having the substance of consciousness.
True Suchness (tathatā) is the object of cognition (ālambana). This is the Dharma; the Dharma and that which possesses the Dharma are termed the thesis (pakṣa).

However, because they arise following the marks of the signless object, because they follow after the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-vikalpa), and because they are conditioned (saṃskṛta), these three are all established reasons (hetu). And because they follow [the signless]...

Regarding the phrase "because the characteristics of the object and the arising of the characteristics [occur]": although you claim that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) exists by means of conceptual construction, even while being separated from the two parts of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka*), it nevertheless arises in accordance with the characteristics of the object and the arising of the characteristics of those two parts.

If there is a cognizing wisdom (*ālambaka-jñāna*) and an object of cognition (*ālambana*), how can it be called non-conceptual wisdom if it does not transcend conceptual construction, even though its object is the true realm devoid of marks (*animitta-tattva-viṣaya*)?

Regarding the phrase "because it is followed by intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*)," this non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), if it relies upon the first dhyāna, as well as the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) or the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), will necessarily be followed by vitarka and vicāra; therefore, it is said to be "followed by intrinsic discrimination.
Furthermore, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is also termed "intrinsic discrimination. Thus, although your non-conceptual wisdom is not an inference (*anumāna*), [it is still subject to this].

Regarding discriminative wisdom (*vikalpa-jñāna*): there is discriminative wisdom that functions as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and that which is subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) may also be discriminative.

Taking *tathatā* (suchness) as its objective sphere (*ālambana-svabhāva*), it is precisely that which acts as the subject of discrimination. It is the wisdom whose nature is *tathatā* that is subsequently attained;

this is a case of the function following the essence. As for the phrase "because it is conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*): since you consider this non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to be the subject...

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): True Suchness (*tathatā*) is taken as the object-condition because both are *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Therefore, it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Just like other forms of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) involving conceptual cognition (*savikalpa-buddhi*), it does not constitute supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

[The passage on] hearing the Dharma through analogies is like other forms of direct perception involving conceptual cognition; as long as they persist within the cognitive domain, they do not constitute supramundane non-conceptual wisdom. You, now...
What has been stated also exists within the domain of wisdom; how can it alone be considered merely discursive cognition? Second, regarding the inference (*anumāna*):

that which you postulate as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—the *tathatā* (suchness) free from characteristics and free from verbal expression—is the thesis (*pakṣa*). Because it is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), it is the reason (*hetu*), just like other objects of cognition.

It does not constitute the ultimate reality; this is the example by similarity (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*), just like the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that are the objects of the other five consciousnesses.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*) and the meditative object: at the very moment a single moment of consciousness correctly apprehends an object, this object is likewise devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and beyond words (*nirabhilāpya*).
Since it does not thereby constitute the meaning of true reality (*tattva*), why should only this present object of cognition alone be established as the supreme ultimate (*paramārtha-tathatā*)?
Second, for this reason, both are equally not the most excellent; that is to say, by means of the two aforementioned types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one realizes their corresponding [nature].
The Master’s statement that non-conceptuality is not the most supreme is as follows. In the section below on the Sūtras, the second part cites scriptures as proof.

The first scripture proves that the wisdom which takes the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) as its object is [non-conceptual]; the subsequent scripture proves that there is no objective referent to be experienced.
Based on this reasoning and scriptural authority, the third section concludes the refutation of the fixed adherence to practice.
By means of these two principles established through inference and the two scriptural citations adduced, those masters who correspond [to our position] should abandon their fixed attachment—
within the realization of non-conceptual wisdom and the ultimate truth— to the imagined existence of both the cognizing subject (the wisdom) and the cognized object (true suchness).

Furthermore, examining the following, the second section refutes the very essence of cognition (*jñāna*). This passage contains two parts. First, it establishes a syllogism to refute what has been asserted:
that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is also not substantially existent. This is the formal proposition (*pratijñā*), which states:

"I shall now further [argue] that, according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), such as you have described, the wisdom that possesses an objective support (*ālambana*) and an object of cognition (*ālambanīya*) does not exist within the supramundane stage."
A distinct cognition. This cognition, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), is likewise not substantially existent, because it arises from conditions;
it is like an illusory person. This is the illustration by way of shared characteristics (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*). The remainder of the text is intelligible. Second, "if cognition can sever...

and so forth, refutes their assertion that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*) can sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). That is to say, if one asserts that non-conceptual cognition can sever [afflictions]...
Regarding delusions, one thus firmly maintains that wisdom can sever them. Yet this wisdom which performs the severing is itself like those delusions it severs.
Why? Because it possesses faults; specifically, because there is the fault of the one who maintains such a position.
Therefore, I shall no longer point out these faults. If one were to establish an inference (*anumāna*) to demonstrate the fault, one should say: "It is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)."
Wisdom cannot be deludedly established as a thesis because it arises from conditions; this is the reason for the establishment [of the thesis].

It may also be like other conceptual wisdoms, and likewise like an illusion; these are the similes of "sameness of dharma" (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta), which can be understood according to what was stated previously. Therefore, they are not explicitly set forth here.
Fourth, once such attachments as these have been eliminated, there follows the explanation of the method for cultivating and giving rise to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-prajñā*).
This section contains three parts: first, the explanation of the characteristics of wisdom; second, from "The practitioner of meditation...

onwards, the explanation of the perfection of the practice of wisdom and its confirmation by the Buddha; third, from "This practice of wisdom is called noble silence... onwards, the explanation of non-... [text ends].
The wisdom of discernment (*pravicaya-prajñā*) has various distinct names. Within the preceding section, there are two parts: first, the formal elucidation of the practice and understanding;

second, from "As the Blessed One said" onwards, citing scriptures as proof. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, concluding by removing the aforementioned faults, hence the statement: "Thus, once these attachments have been eliminated...
Second, from "Regarding that which should be known" onwards, establishing a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) to clarify the practice. This refers to "that which should be known..."

"The nature of the object is likewise devoid of cognitive activity (*pratipatti*). This is the thesis (*pakṣa*), meaning that the object lacks intrinsic nature and characteristics, and cognition lacks cognitive activity.

"Because the conditions for [the arising of] the object are absent," this is the reason (*hetu*). That is to say, the object gives rise to cognitive activity; thus, the object is the causal condition (*pratyaya*) for cognitive activity.
Now, one should understand that since the object already lacks intrinsic nature and characteristics, by what cause could the cognizing cognitive activity arise? Therefore, it is said:
This is because the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*) are lacking. The fact that other cognitions do not arise due to the absence of mental application (*abhisamaya*) serves as a parallel example.

For instance, when a cognition apprehends an object, there is first the external object; then, within the three realms of existence, there are simultaneous factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, which constitute the mental application. Thus, there are three [factors].

Since there is the arising of wisdom together with the mental application (*manasikāra*) of feeling and so forth, because they are all factors of enumeration (*saṃskāra*), if there were no objective referent (*ālambana-viṣaya*), then there would be no mental application.
Since mental application would be absent, wisdom would not arise. Now, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise:
if the object lacks intrinsic nature and characteristics, then mental application does not occur. Since mental application does not arise, by what means could wisdom [arise]?
"Because the three [realms] are born [from this], it is called 'true practice and understanding' (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*).
Regarding form and so forth: the object is devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics, and is thus not that which is grasped; practice and understanding do not function, and there is no grasper.

Although there is indeed no practice and understanding here, practice and understanding are ultimately such; although practice and understanding are manifest, they are without practice and understanding. Therefore, it is named 'true practice and understanding.'"

Second, "As the World-Honored One said" and below, citations from the sūtras are provided as proof. There are five sections in this passage: first, the sūtra clarifies practice and realization (*caryā-adhigama*);

Once the cultivation of wisdom has been realized, it is established through six aspects of practice. First, "clearly understanding the realization of practice" (*prajñā-sākṣātkriyā-pratipatti*).
Second, from "thus correctly contemplating" (*evam samyak-paśyan*) onwards, this refers to the extensive explanation in the Sūtra which exhorts beings to give rise to faith.

By contemplating all phenomena as being identical—neither arising nor perceived—one is able to abandon the false views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding the characteristics of existence and non-existence within the *dharmatā*. Therefore, it is called "right view. This constitutes the realization of the equality of all phenomena.

When pervasive conceptualization has forever ceased and erroneous thoughts do not arise, it is called "right reflection. Because one realizes non-arising, all seeking, questioning, mental formations, and frivolous speech are forever stilled;
this is called "right speech. Since phenomena are equal and devoid of arising or activity, one is free from the three types of erroneous karma of body, speech, and mind;
this is called "right action. By realizing that all things possess a nature of neither increase nor decrease, one knows...

To have no [wrong] livelihood and to be free from improper desires is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). To realize that all phenomena are without action and without arising, and to be free from improper striving and seeking, is called right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
To realize that the nature of phenomena transcends existence and non-existence, and to be free from improper deluded thoughts, is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
To realize that all phenomena are without anything to be grasped, and to be free from improper reliance and dwelling, is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Below...
The explanation of the "fingers" [as metaphors] can be understood.

Regarding the passage "Thus, through correct contemplation," which clarifies that once wisdom has been cultivated, one realizes and establishes the six modes of conduct (*ṣaḍ-ākāra*), there are three sections in the text. First is the conclusion of the preceding and the introduction of the subsequent.

As for the phrase "although [the text] speaks of the six modes of conduct, it does not [speak of] the six matters": this refers to the fact that within a single moment of thought, there is no differentiation.
The distinct wisdom [of generosity] is fully endowed with the six modes of practice;

it does not mean that one must first cultivate preparatory application (*prayoga*) before it arises. Therefore, it is said that although there are these matters, giving has the meaning of abandoning wealth and departing from stinginess.
When wisdom realizes [the truth], it abandons conditioned activity and discards delusion; it is likewise so. Precepts take the cessation of evil and self-restraint as their meaning;
when wisdom realizes [the truth], conditions cease and there is nothing to be attained; it is likewise so. Patience takes the cessation of anger and the arising of compassion as its meaning;
when wisdom realizes [the truth], one realizes the non-arising of dharmas and does not tolerate arising; it is likewise so. Realizing the dharma...
Non-arising: anger does not arise; one does not tolerate arising. Compassion without conditions is established. Diligence takes the meaning of unremitting progress and seeking as its essence.
At the time of realization through wisdom, there is equality. In this equality, one does not grasp at superior practices, nor does one abandon [inferior ones].

It is also like this. The meaning of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is for the mind to abide in stillness. When wisdom realizes it, there is nothing capable of causing the mind to dwell [on anything];
it is also like this. The meaning of perfect knowledge (*prajñā*) is to cease conceptual discrimination and remain far removed from delusion.
When wisdom realizes it, the wisdom of discrimination does not arise, so that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) does not occur; all objects are equal.
...and so forth. Thus, one remains far removed from the two marks. Regarding "this meaning" below, the location where it is explained can be understood.

Thirdly, regarding "thus abiding in the wondrous" below, this is a general praise of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) as that which guides all practices, exhorting beings to cultivate and study it.
Although the text near at hand praises non-conceptual wisdom, it distantly encompasses the entire section as an exhortation for beings to circulate [the teaching]. It says: "Thus wondrous..."
Regarding "dwelling in immeasurable gateways": non-conceptual wisdom abandons [the distinctions between] superior and inferior.
According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is neither superior nor inferior; it is only in accordance with [conventional reality] that one speaks of superior and inferior.
As for what is called "dwelling," it is the realization of equality by wisdom. Furthermore, in relation to what is this "dwelling" spoken of? This then—
It is not abiding, yet it is forcibly designated as "abiding"; this is precisely the non-abiding of the abiding of abiding.

However, when this wisdom of wondrous abiding is realized through direct proof, immeasurable Dharma-gates are taught according to their respective meanings. Throughout the various Bodhisattva-piṭaka sūtras, the Buddha has explained this extensively in many places.
When realizing this wisdom of proof, there is great benefit and significance; that is to say, the realization of Great Nirvāṇa.

"Vast" (*pāṇa*) refers to the great meaning (*mahārtha*). "Realizing great enlightenment" (*mahābodhi*) refers to the great benefit (*mahālābha*), because through the wisdom that penetrates enlightenment, one is endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*) and is able to benefit both oneself and others.
This is thus taking what is not meaning or benefit as meaning and benefit. The exhortation for beings to practice and study this can be understood through explanation.
